implementation_notes: std ships the guard, not the lazy object: store a OnceLock<Image> in the stand-in and call get_or_init(|| Image::load(&path)) from the accessor, so the closure runs once even when threads race and every caller sees the same reference. Unlike the static-oriented LazyLock, OnceLock works per instance and its get() answers 'was it ever built?' without forcing construction, which is what lifecycle and diagnostic code needs. A panic propagates to the caller and leaves the cell uninitialized, so the next caller retries; reentrant initialization is documented as an error that currently deadlocks, and the accessor keeps the classic proxy class unnecessary unless several interface methods must be forwarded.
pitfalls: get_or_init must not re-enter the same cell: the documented outcome for reentrant initialization is unspecified and currently deadlocks.
A panicking initializer leaves the cell uninitialized, so the next access retries; if that is not wanted, cache the error beside the cell instead of relying on once semantics.
OnceLock is not Sync unless T: Send + Sync, and it makes the stand-in neither Copy nor trivially cloneable - sharing the built value across threads constrains both T and the container.

variants.name: std::sync::LazyLock for a process-wide subject
variants.implementation_notes: LazyLock is the deref-shaped sibling: `static IMAGE: LazyLock<Image> = LazyLock::new(|| Image::load(PATH));` initializes on the first dereference and every later use looks like a reference to the value, which is the cleanest shape for a process-wide subject. It blocks any dereferencing thread while another thread is initializing, and it cannot take extra inputs after new(), so per-instance or parameterized construction stays with OnceLock. Choose it for process-wide singletons whose construction needs no runtime arguments; note that statics are never dropped, so the subject's destructor does not run.
pitfalls: Every deref blocks while the initializer runs, so a slow construction serializes all readers even after startup.
Statics are never dropped: the subject's destructor does not run at exit, so resources that need explicit release must be closed by hand.
LazyLock::new cannot receive per-instance inputs, and a poisoned initializer panics every future access - parameterized or fallible construction belongs behind OnceLock.

variants.name: once_cell crate (pre-std and unsync flavours)
variants.implementation_notes: Before OnceLock and LazyLock were stabilized the once_cell crate was the standard route: sync::Lazy for statics and sync::OnceCell / unsync::OnceCell for owned slots, with get_or_init mirroring the std API today. The unsync flavour is the interesting extra - it skips atomics entirely for stand-ins that never cross threads, where std has no equivalent (OnceLock is always thread-safe). Choose the crate when the MSRV is pinned below 1.70, or when the single-threaded cell is a measurable win; otherwise the std types are equivalent and dependency-free.
pitfalls: unsync::OnceCell is not Sync: using it behind a shared reference across threads does not compile, so it only fits stand-ins confined to one thread.
Mixing once_cell types with std OnceLock/LazyLock in one codebase duplicates the abstraction and confuses which guarantees apply; migrate rather than sprinkle both.
Lazy's deref behaves like a reference, so mutating the stored subject still requires interior mutability (Mutex/RwLock), exactly as with the std types.
